pos: n. (the Hampshire Cistercian abbey of 1239, the most complete surviving Cistercian church in southern England)
etymology: Old English naet and leah, the wet clearing, through Middle English Letley; Latinised Laetus Locus, the glad place.
biblical_def: Netley Abbey on Southampton Water was begun in 1239 with money left by Peter des Roches, bishop of Winchester, and completed under the patronage of Henry III, whose arms it carried. It was never rich; its monks petitioned more than once about poverty and the cost of hospitality to travellers landing nearby. Dissolved in 1536, it was granted to Sir William Paulet, who turned the church into a Tudor mansion, and when that was abandoned the shell became the best-preserved Cistercian church in the south of England and one of the most visited ruins in the country, drawing eighteenth-century poets and painters who came to feel melancholy among the arches. The dictionary records Netley for that second career, because a ruin admired for its atmosphere has been put to a use the builders never intended and the gospel does not endorse. Sentiment about old stones is not devotion. “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) locates worship in the worshipper and the truth, and “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) tells a Christian what to expect of every building he admires.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; melancholy as a gloomy state of mind; picturesque as pleasing to the eye in the manner of a picture; hospitality as the entertainment of strangers; and continuing as lasting.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house, or any work of men.
MELANCHOLY, n. A gloomy state of mind, often a gloomy state that is of some continuance.
PICTURESQUE, a. Expressing that peculiar kind of beauty which is agreeable in a picture.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely.
scriptures: Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Hampshire Cistercian abbey begun 1239, dissolved 1536, whose shell became the best-preserved Cistercian church in southern England.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reverence has an object. Netley's visitors came for a mood, and Christ fixes worship elsewhere: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24). A ruin may be beautiful without being holy, and the distinction is not a quibble.

The live temptation is to mistake nostalgia for faith, which an abbey-shaped ruin makes easy. Hebrews gives the Christian his expectation about buildings plainly, “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14), and directs the longing somewhere it will be met, “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). The men of faith held that posture lifelong, “strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

“a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10) — where the longing is actually met.

pos: n. (the New Forest Cistercian abbey founded by King John in 1203, whose account book of 1269 survives)
etymology: Norman French beau lieu, the beautiful place, Latinised Bellus Locus Regis; the English pronunciation has long been anglicised.
biblical_def: Beaulieu Abbey in the New Forest was founded in 1203 by King John, by tradition in expiation of a quarrel with the Cistercian order, and it became one of the largest Cistercian houses in England with granges scattered across Hampshire and Wiltshire. Two things make it unusual. Its account book for 1269 and 1270 survives entire, and it is among the finest records anywhere of how a large medieval estate was actually run — stock, wool, tilery, salt, and the accounting between the granges. And its precinct held a right of sanctuary that was used, notably by Perkin Warbeck's followers in 1497 and by Margaret of Anjou in 1471. The abbey was dissolved in 1538; its refectory survives as the parish church. The dictionary records Beaulieu for the sanctuary, which is the medieval church's most attractive institution and its most instructive. The impulse was right: Scripture does appoint places of refuge. But the refuge Scripture finally names is a person, and “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28) is an invitation no precinct wall can imitate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sanctuary as a sacred place, and a place of protection; a grange as a farm with its buildings; an account as a registry of debt and credit; refuge as shelter from danger; and expiation as atonement.
webster_full: SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple; a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; in England, a farm belonging to a monastery.
ACCOUNT, n. A registry of debt and credit; a computation of debts and credits, or of receipts and payments.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
EXPIATION, n. The act of atoning for a crime; the means by which atonement is made.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Large New Forest Cistercian abbey founded by King John in 1203, with a surviving estate account book and a used right of sanctuary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the refuge is a person. Beaulieu's walls sheltered the hunted, which was a real mercy, and the gospel offers the thing the walls were imitating: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28). Isaiah describes the rest that follows, “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee” (Isa 26:3), and it depends on a mind stayed rather than a boundary respected.

The live temptation is to read sanctuary as proof that the system was fundamentally merciful and so needed no reform. The mercy was genuine, and so is James' standard for it, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). But an abbey founded in expiation of a king's quarrel is also the system's theology in one sentence, and that theology falls to “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

“Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) — what an expiatory foundation falls to.

pos: n. (the Isle of Wight abbey founded 1132, Savigniac then Cistercian, refounded in 1908 by exiled French Benedictines)
etymology: From the limestone quarries beside the site, Middle English quarrere; Latinised Quarraria.
biblical_def: Quarr Abbey on the Isle of Wight was founded in 1132 by Baldwin de Redvers for monks of Savigny, absorbed with the rest of that order into the Cistercians in 1147, and named from the limestone quarries beside it that supplied stone for Winchester and Chichester. It was dissolved in 1536 and the buildings were almost entirely demolished for their material. Quarr has an unusual second chapter: in 1908 Benedictine monks expelled from Solesmes by French anticlerical legislation settled nearby and built a new Quarr Abbey of Belgian brick to designs by one of their own number, Dom Paul Bellot, a building now reckoned among the most original religious works of its century. The dictionary records Quarr for the pair of them, and declines to be sentimental about either. The 1908 community came as refugees from a hostile state, which deserves sympathy, and it came holding the same account of the religious life the Reformers refused. “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) is said to all Christians and “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3) names the vow's error without any licence for the law that expelled them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a quarry as a place where stones are dug; an exile as one banished from his country; brick as a mass of clay burnt; an order as a religious fraternity; and liberty as freedom from restraint.
webster_full: QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; the person banished.
BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine, then formed into a long square and baked.
ORDER, n. A religious fraternity or society; a body of men united by some common rule.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint; the power of acting as one thinks fit, without any restraint but the laws of nature.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Joh 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Isle of Wight abbey of 1132, demolished after 1536, with a new abbey built nearby in 1908 by Benedictines exiled from Solesmes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the doctrinal objection and the civil one are separate. Peter's description of the Christian people admits no spiritual caste, “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9), and Paul names the specific error of the vow, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3). That is the dictionary's disagreement with Quarr, old and new.

The live temptation is to let the disagreement license the French laws that drove the Solesmes community out in 1901. It does not. Christ makes truth the liberator, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32), and a state that expels monks has not advanced it. What Scripture asks of a church is its own good government, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40), not the suppression of a neighbour's.

pos: n. (the monastery in County Louth founded by Buithe, famed for Muiredach's high cross)
etymology: Irish Mainistir Bhuithe, the monastery of Buithe, its sixth-century founder.
biblical_def: Monasterboice in County Louth was founded by Buithe, who died about 521, and it kept a school of some reputation into the twelfth century before the Cistercians at nearby Mellifont drew its life away. What remains is a round tower, two ruined churches, and three high crosses, of which Muiredach's Cross is the finest sculptured cross in Ireland. It is carved over its whole surface with scenes: the fall, Cain and Abel, David and Goliath, Moses striking the rock, the adoration of the magi, the arrest of Christ, and a great Last Judgment on the head. The dictionary records Monasterboice for that cross, because it is a serious attempt to put Scripture where unlettered people could get at it, and the attempt deserves the credit. It is also the limit of the method. A carving can show that Moses struck a rock; it cannot say why, and “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) describes something words do. Hence the apostolic emphasis falls on hearing: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the preacher is the appointed instrument, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cross as a monument in the form of a cross; sculpture as the art of carving; unlettered as untaught; imagery as sensible representations; and a judgment as a final determination.
webster_full: CROSS, n. A gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other; a monument with a cross erected to excite devotion.
SCULPTURE, n. The art of carving, cutting or hewing wood or stone into images.
UNLETTERED, a. Unlearned; untaught; ignorant; not instructed in science or literature.
IMAGERY, n. Sensible representations, pictures, statues; forms of the fancy; false ideas.
JUDGMENT, n. The act of determining, as in courts of law; the final trial of the human race.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: County Louth monastery founded by Buithe before 521, site of Muiredach's Cross, the finest sculptured high cross in Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the proper credit and the proper limit of a carved Bible. Muiredach's Cross puts the fall and the judgment in front of people who could not read, and the aim is the Psalmist's, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130). The stone deserves respect for trying.

The live temptation is to treat images as equivalent to the word, which the medieval church increasingly did. The appointed means is not visual: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and God's chosen folly is a man speaking, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). The pattern that actually works is Nehemiah's, where they “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8) — read, explained, and caused the people to understand.

pos: n. (the County Laois monastery of Canice, once the see of Ossory)
etymology: Irish Achadh Bho, the field of the cow; the cow element is in the earliest annals.
biblical_def: Aghaboe in County Laois was founded in the sixth century by Canice, the saint whose name Kilkenny carries, and it became the principal church of the kingdom of Ossory and the seat of its bishops until the see was transferred to Kilkenny in the twelfth century. Aghaboe kept the relics of Canice and a school; it was burned more than once, by Vikings and by Irish rivals, and in 1382 a Dominican friary was established on the site. Little stands now beyond the friary ruin and a fragment of the earlier church. The dictionary records Aghaboe for the transfer of the see, because the moving of a bishop's chair from the saint's field to the growing town shows what the office had become: a jurisdiction attached to a place and a revenue. Scripture's bishop is a different thing altogether — a man who feeds a congregation, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and whose qualification is a grip on a text, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). The relics stayed at Aghaboe; the duty was never in them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a see as the seat of episcopal power; a bishop as an overseer; a diocese as the circuit of a bishop's jurisdiction; a flock as a company of the faithful; and translation as the removal of a bishop to another see.
webster_full: SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director; an elder.
DIOCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection; applied to sheep and other small animals; a Christian church.
TRANSLATION, n. The removal of a bishop from one see to another.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Sixth-century monastery of Canice in County Laois, see of Ossory until the chair moved to Kilkenny in the twelfth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what a bishop is for. Paul tells the Ephesian elders their business in one clause, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and tells Titus what qualifies a man for it, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9). Neither sentence mentions a chair, a town, or a saint's bones.

The live temptation is to think the office is constituted by its seat, which is exactly what the move to Kilkenny assumed. Malachi's picture of the ministry is a man carrying knowledge, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7), and the church's arrangements exist to serve that, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40), not to outrank a neighbouring field.

pos: n. (the County Tipperary monastery of Cronan, source of the eighth-century Book of Dimma)
etymology: Irish Ros Cre, the wood of Cre; the personal or place element Cre is obscure.
biblical_def: Roscrea in County Tipperary grew up around the monastery of Cronan, who moved his community in the early seventh century from a secluded spot to the roadside so that travellers could find it — a detail his life records with approval. The site keeps a round tower, a high cross, and the west gable of a twelfth-century Romanesque church. Its chief treasure is portable: the Book of Dimma, a small eighth-century pocket gospel book written at Roscrea, with the four Gospels and an order for the visitation of the sick, now in Trinity College Dublin. A Franciscan friary was founded in the town in 1490. The dictionary records Roscrea for Cronan's move and for Dimma's book together, since both are decisions about access. A monastery placed where travellers pass and a Gospel small enough to carry to a sickbed are the same instinct, and it is the right one. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) sends the church outward, and “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) will not wait for a convenient season.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gospel as the history of Christ; a pocket as a small bag; visitation as the act of visiting the sick; a traveller as one who journeys; and instant as pressing or urgent.
webster_full: GOSPEL, n. The history of the birth, life, actions, death, resurrection, ascension and doctrine of Jesus Christ.
POCKET, n. A small bag inserted in a garment for carrying small articles.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; the visiting of the sick and afflicted by a minister of the gospel.
TRAVELER, n. One who travels; one who passes from place to place, either for pleasure, for business, or for health.
INSTANT, a. Pressing; urgent; importunate; earnest.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: County Tipperary monastery of Cronan, moved to the roadside for travellers, where the pocket-sized Book of Dimma was written in the eighth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is access. Cronan moved his house to the road and Dimma wrote a Gospel a man could carry, and both serve the commission as it stands: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19). Paul's charge allows no waiting for better conditions, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

The live temptation is to admire the artistry of Irish gospel books and forget that this one was made for a sickbed. A small book with an order for visiting the sick is pastoral equipment, aimed at the same thing the Lord offers directly, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Mat 11:28). The standing duty behind it is simply “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13).

pos: n. (the island monastery in Lough Leane, Killarney, where the Annals of Inisfallen were written)
etymology: Irish Inis Faithlenn, the island of Faithlenn; the anglicised spelling varies between Innisfallen and Inisfallen.
biblical_def: Inisfallen is a wooded island in Lough Leane at Killarney, where a monastery was founded in the seventh century, traditionally by Finian the Leper, and continued as an Augustinian priory until its suppression in the sixteenth century. Its importance is a manuscript. The Annals of Inisfallen, begun on the island about 1092 and continued there by successive hands into the fourteenth century, are one of the principal sources for early Irish history, and the earlier portion draws on a world chronicle to set Irish events in a wider frame. The dictionary records Inisfallen for the annals, because keeping a dated record is a discipline the Bible itself practises and commends. Scripture is full of regnal years and genealogies, and “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) makes the writing down a deliberate service to people not yet born. “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.” (Psa 145:4) describes the handing on, and “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) states what the records are finally for: our learning, not our antiquarianism.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines annals as a history in order of time; a chronicle as a register of events; a genealogy as an account of descent; a generation as a single succession; and learning as acquired knowledge.
webster_full: ANNALS, n. A species of history digested in order of time, or a relation of events in chronological order, each event being recorded under the year in which it happened.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors in the natural order of succession.
GENERATION, n. A single succession of natural descent, as the children of the same parents; a race.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
Job 8:8
For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers:
corruption_summary: Island monastery in Lough Leane where the Annals of Inisfallen were written from about 1092 into the fourteenth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that recording is a service to the unborn. The Psalmist says so of his own text, “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18), and describes the chain it is meant to travel down, “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.” (Psa 145:4). Monks copying dated entries on a lake island for three centuries were doing something Scripture does on purpose.

The live temptation is antiquarianism — the record kept for its own sake. Paul states the purpose and it is instructional, “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4). Job's friend recommends the same enquiry, “enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers” (Job 8:8), as a means to an end and not a hobby.

Hebrew dor (H1755) — a generation, an age; “enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers”, Job 8:8.

“whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) — the purpose is instruction.
“enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers” (Job 8:8) — enquiry as a means, not a hobby.

pos: n. (the Sligo island monastery of Molaise, with an intact cashel and the cursing stones)
etymology: Irish Inis Muiredach, the island of Muiredach, anglicised through Inismurry.
biblical_def: Inishmurray lies four miles off the Sligo coast. A monastery was founded there in the sixth century, attributed to Molaise, and it was plundered by Vikings in 807. What survives is the most complete early monastic enclosure in Ireland: a massive dry-stone cashel with internal chambers, three oratories, beehive cells, stone altars and slab-shrines, all within the wall. On one altar lie the clocha breaca, the speckled stones, which island tradition held could be turned while a curse was pronounced against an enemy, and which were still being so used within living memory of the island's evacuation in 1948. The dictionary records Inishmurray for those stones, because they are the clearest surviving case in these islands of Christian furniture put to frankly magical use. Scripture forbids it without qualification and supplies the alternative in the same breath. Prayer is petition to a Person who hears, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), and the worship God requires is “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) — neither of which a turned stone can counterfeit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a curse as an imprecation of evil; divination as the act of foretelling by supernatural means; superstition as excessive exactness in religious opinions; an amulet as a charm worn to prevent evil; and sorcery as magic.
webster_full: CURSE, n. Malediction; the expression of a wish of evil to another; imprecation of evil.
DIVINATION, n. The act of divining; a foretelling future events, or discovering things secret, by the aid of superior beings, or by other than human means.
SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; belief in the direct agency of superior powers in certain extraordinary or singular events.
AMULET, n. Something worn as a remedy or preservative against evils or mischief, such as charms and spells.
SORCERY, n. Magic; enchantment; witchcraft; divination by the assistance of evil spirits.
scriptures: Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: Sixth-century island monastery off Sligo with Ireland's most complete monastic cashel, and the cursing stones used into the twentieth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between prayer and magic. Prayer addresses a Person who hears in secret, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), and the worship He requires is specified, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24). A stone turned to deliver a curse is a mechanism, and mechanisms are what paganism offers.

The live temptation is to call the speckled stones harmless folk colour. Paul's warning covers precisely this kind of accretion, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8), where a tradition of men is grafted onto Christian furniture. The remedy he gives a congregation is the plain one: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).
roots_summary: Greek kruptos (G2927), secret; Greek pneuma (G4151), spirit; Greek paradosis (G3862), tradition; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test.
roots_lines: Greek kruptos (G2927) — hidden, secret; “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret”, Matthew 6:6.
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath; “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”, John 4:24.
Greek aletheia (G0225) — truth; “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”, John 4:24.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition, that handed down; “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men”, Colossians 2:8.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, to test; “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
usage: “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) — prayer addresses a Person, not a mechanism.
“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8) — the warning covers exactly this accretion.
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) — the remedy given to a congregation.

pos: n. (the Shannon estuary island monastery of Senan, with its round tower)
etymology: From Irish Inis Cathaigh, the island of Cathach, through Norse and English forms to Scattery.
biblical_def: Scattery Island, Inis Cathaigh, lies in the Shannon estuary off Kilrush, and a monastery was founded there in the sixth century by Senan, whose legend has him expelling a monster from the island before he could settle it. The site keeps the remains of several churches and one of the tallest round towers in Ireland, with its doorway at ground level, unusually. Its position made it valuable and vulnerable: Vikings seized it as a base in the tenth century, and it changed hands repeatedly between Norse and Irish before passing under the bishops of Killaloe. The dictionary records Scattery for the round tower, which is the standard Irish monastic answer to raiding — a bell tower that doubled as a refuge and a strongroom. It was a sensible precaution and it was not a defence of anything that mattered. A tower keeps books and plate; the faith it housed is kept otherwise. “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) is the right question, and the answer Scripture gives is a stone no raider reaches, “a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tower as a lofty building; a refuge as shelter from danger; plunder as spoil taken by force; a foundation as the basis of an edifice; and a corner stone as the stone uniting two walls.
webster_full: TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
PLUNDER, n. That which is taken from an enemy by force; pillage; prey; spoil.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of an edifice which lies on the ground.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
scriptures: Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: Sixth-century monastery of Senan on an island in the Shannon estuary, with one of Ireland's tallest round towers; held for a time by Vikings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what can and cannot be defended by masonry. Scattery's tower saved books and vessels from raiders, which was worth doing. The Psalmist asks the deeper question, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3), and the answer is laid elsewhere: “a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16).

The live temptation is to measure a church's security by its walls, which is the instinct every fortified monastery encouraged. Paul forecloses it, “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and Hebrews tells the Christian what to expect of any stronghold he builds, “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

usage: “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) — the deeper question a tower cannot answer.
“a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16) — a stone no raider reaches.
“here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — what to expect of any stronghold.

pos: n. (the County Mayo see traditionally founded by Patrick, with its round tower)
etymology: Irish Cill Ala, the church of Ala or Alaidh; the first element is cill, a church, as in many Irish place names.
biblical_def: Killala in County Mayo is by tradition one of the churches Patrick founded, and the annals record him appointing Muiredach as its first bishop. It became the see of a diocese covering north Mayo and west Sligo, and it has carried bishops of one communion or another ever since; the Church of Ireland cathedral of St Patrick stands on the site, and beside it a well-preserved round tower of the twelfth century. The town is remembered in Irish history for a later episode, the landing of a French expedition in support of the rising of 1798. The dictionary records Killala for the Patrician foundation, and takes the occasion to say what the dictionary thinks of Patrick. His own Confession is the earliest document written in Ireland and it is a plainly scriptural book: he calls himself a sinner, he quotes the Bible constantly, and he describes his mission as obedience to the commission. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) is his warrant in his own account, and “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11) is his confidence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a see as the seat of a bishop; a cathedral as the principal church of a diocese; a confession as an acknowledgment; a commission as a charge or warrant; and a round tower is given under tower as a lofty building.
webster_full: SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
CATHEDRAL, n. The see or seat of a bishop; the principal church in a diocese.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime or fault; a profession of belief in the articles of faith.
COMMISSION, n. The act of committing or entrusting; a warrant or written authority for performing an office.
TOWER, n. A building raised to a considerable elevation above the adjacent ground or buildings.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
corruption_summary: County Mayo see traditionally founded by Patrick, who appointed Muiredach its first bishop; its round tower and cathedral stand together.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Patrick as he presents himself. His Confession is not hagiography but a scriptural self-accounting, and the commission he claims is the one in Matthew, “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19). His confidence is Isaiah's, that the word sent out “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

The live temptation is the accumulated legend — the snakes, the shamrock, the staff — which has nearly replaced the man and his book. The remedy is to read what he wrote, and what he wrote sounds like Paul: “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16). The charge he obeyed is the plain one, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).
